name: Gareth Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Gareth, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, how would you describe your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ruth and I own Copse End, 220 acres on the edge of the downs: 90 suckler cows, seed potatoes and spring barley. We bought it nine years ago with money from her grandmother and a big mortgage. Ruth's a vet at the practice in town, so the farm's mostly me plus a part-timer, Lewis. I also run a small drone business on the side, mapping and spot-spraying for other farms.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start with coffee and the screen: grazing records, potato store temperatures, the weather, and an AI assistant that I ask a dozen questions a day, from what's wrong with a sick calf's photo to drafting a quote for a drone job. Then I'm out moving cattle, fixing fences, in the potato store or flying the drone over someone's oilseed rape. I love solving problems. What wears me out is the gap between what's possible and what I've got time for, and the bank manager's quarterly call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful but overhyped, and those of us who used it well got a bit ahead. I'd post something about it in the farm tech group I'm in, probably a bit smug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, steady. The farm pays, the drone work pays, the mortgage gets paid. I'd be slightly disappointed, I like it when things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I've got and keep building the drone business, maybe buy a second drone and train Lewis to fly it. That's about eight thousand. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a harvest that comes in fine but nothing to write home about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools a lot. Where would that leave you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, slightly ahead of my neighbours. Saving maybe an hour a day on paperwork and planning, which I'd spend on fences.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the drone business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That keeps going too. Farmers want their crops mapped, AI or no AI. In this picture it's just a steady little earner.

S0.say: I'd say it was useful but overhyped, and those who used it well got a bit ahead. I'd post that in my farm tech group, probably a bit smug.
S0.think: For me it's steady: the farm, the drone work and the mortgage all keep going. I'd be slightly disappointed, because I like it when things move.
S0.do: Keeps using his current AI tools and grows the drone business with a second drone, about eight thousand. Trains his part-timer to fly it.
S0.quote: I'd post something about it in the farm tech group I'm in, probably a bit smug.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth is an early adopter who's a bit let down when nothing changes. His drone business gives him a second income and a sense of being ahead. He's practical and doesn't take strong political positions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on with it. The farms that adapt will do well, the ones that don't will struggle. I'd say that at the discussion group and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. I'm already halfway there. And the drone business would grow because everyone would want the kit and someone to show them how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a robot fencing and grazing system and an automated potato grader, maybe 60 to 70 thousand, with a bank loan and some savings. I'd push the drone business into a full advisory service for neighbours. That's my first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It's the kind of puzzle I like, with a bank loan attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you buy first, and how much would it cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grader first. It's twelve weeks a year of the most boring job on the farm. About 35 thousand, and it'd pay for itself in four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Lewis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lewis would move up to running the machines with me. He's 24 and keen. I'd pay him more, not less.

S1.say: I'd say get on with it, because farms that adapt will do well and the rest will struggle. I'd say that at my discussion group and online.
S1.think: I think it's good for me, as I'm already halfway there. The drone business would grow because everyone would want help with the kit.
S1.do: Buys a robot grazing system and an automated potato grader for 60 to 70 thousand using a loan and savings. Expands the drone business into a full advisory service for neighbours.
S1.quote: It's twelve weeks a year of the most boring job on the farm.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth sees this as an opportunity and moves fast, borrowing to invest. He'd bring his young worker along and pay him more. His drone side business positions him as the local helper for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be messy, so let's be practical. I'd probably post about what farmers should buy and what they should hold off on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I own land and machines, so I'm probably on the right side of it. But the drone business disappears overnight, because the robots do it themselves. And if nobody has a job, who buys the beef?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy as much robot kit as I could afford in the first six months, before prices jump. I'd keep a year's cash for safety. I'd pay down the farm mortgage with whatever's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, more for how fast everything else shifts. It's like watching a flood come down the valley when your own house is on the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. Does the speed worry you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not so much for me. I've got land and I'm quick. But the speed means half the people I know won't keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother, Tom. He's a lorry driver, and that's gone in two years. I'd offer him something on the farm, even if a robot could do it.

S2.say: I'd say this is going to be messy, so let's be practical. I'd post about what farmers should buy and what to hold off on.
S2.think: I own land and machines, so I'm probably on the right side of it. But the drone business would vanish and I'd wonder who buys the beef if nobody has a job.
S2.do: Buys as much robot kit as he can in the first six months before prices rise and keeps a year's cash for safety. Pays down the farm mortgage with what's left.
S2.feel: Uneasy, more about how fast everything around him shifts than about himself.
S2.quote: If nobody has a job, who buys the beef?
S2.fieldNote: Gareth sees himself as a winner here because he owns land and machines, but he quickly spots the problem of customers losing income. He worries about his brother more than himself. Even fast AGI only makes him uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get it right, so let's plan. I'd want the discussion group to talk about it every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm fine. Five years is enough to switch the farm over properly and maybe help a few neighbours do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Years one and two, I'd buy the kit as it gets proven and cheaper. Year three or four, I'd shift the drone business into helping other farms set up robot systems. I'd talk to Ruth about her practice too, because vets will feel this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'd have a spreadsheet for it by the weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'm not rushing. I can buy at the right price, not the panic price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ella and Josh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to think, not just to do. Ella's into science, Josh into sport. I'd say don't pick a job, pick a skill that goes with you.

S3.say: I'd say we've got time to get it right, so let's plan. I'd want the discussion group talking about it every month.
S3.think: I think I'm fine, because five years is enough to switch the farm over properly. I might help a few neighbours do the same.
S3.do: Buys robot kit as it is proven and gets cheaper in the first two years. Shifts the drone business towards helping other farms set up robots by year three or four, and talks with his partner about her vet practice.
S3.quote: I can buy at the right price, not the panic price.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Gareth relaxes and plans purchases on price rather than speed. He gives his children practical advice about portable skills. He thinks about his partner's work as well as his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's not panic and let's not drag our feet. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the easy one for me. I'd plan, invest, and be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now by paying down the mortgage faster and setting aside money for robot kit. By year five I'd be mostly automated. And I'd keep the farm as a family place, somewhere the kids can come back to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, it feels like a long project, and I like long projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What would you start in 2026?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being needed. I'd miss the days when the farm couldn't run without me, like the night the potato store fan failed and I rewired it at 3am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fixing things. That's the bit I really love, more than the cows if I'm honest. I'd have to find something else to fix.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's not panic and not drag our feet. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.
S4.think: Honestly, this is the easy one for me. I'd plan, invest and be ready well before it arrives.
S4.do: Pays the mortgage down faster now and sets money aside for robot kit. Aims to be mostly automated by year five and keeps the farm as a family place for the children.
S4.feel: Calm, with a quiet sense that he'd miss being needed.
S4.quote: I'd have to find something else to fix.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years makes Gareth fully relaxed about money and planning. His only loss is emotional: he'd miss being needed and fixing things. He thinks of the farm as a family home for the future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but not for me, for everyone else. What would help is a proper safety net for people like my brother, and some way to make sure there are still customers for what farms grow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what people will do all day. I'm fine with robots doing the work, but I don't know what my kids will get up for in the morning.

headlineQuote: I'm fine with robots doing the work, but I don't know what my kids will get up for in the morning.
portrait: Gareth Ziegler is a 43-year-old farmer who owns Copse End, a beef, potato and barley farm, with his vet partner Ruth, and runs a side business flying drones for other farms. He uses AI tools every day and loves solving problems. He stays calm across most pictures because he owns land and machines and moves early, and even fast AGI only makes him uneasy. His worries are for his lorry-driver brother, his customers and what his children will do with their days.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, not for himself but because so many people around him, like his brother, would not keep up.
whatWouldHelp: A proper safety net for people like his brother and a way to make sure there are still customers for what farms grow.
